metaTitle: Bed Bug Bites: What They Look Like (Pictures)
metaDescription: Bed bug bites are usually itchy red welts in a line, zigzag or cluster on skin bare in bed. Pictures, look-alike bites, how long they last, how to confirm.
h1: What Do Bed Bug Bites Look Like? Pictures, Patterns and How to Tell for Sure
dek: Real photos of bites and of the signs that confirm bed bugs, a table against flea, mosquito, chigger and scabies look-alikes, how long bites last, when to see a doctor, and why bites alone never prove bed bugs.
excerpt: What bed bug bites look like, where they show up and how long they last, how to tell them from flea, mosquito and chigger bites, and how to confirm bed bugs before you act.

quickAnswer.lead: **Bed bug bites are usually itchy red welts or inflamed spots, often in a rough line, a zigzag or a small cluster, on skin left bare in bed, such as the face, neck, arms and hands.** They look like many other bites, though: the [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/how-find-bed-bugs) calls bites a poor indicator of an infestation, and only finding bed bugs or their signs confirms them.
bullets: Most people notice marks one to several days after the bite, but they can take as long as 14 days to develop, and some people show no marks at all, the [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/bed-bugs/about/index.html) says.

The [American Academy of Dermatology](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/a-z/bed-bugs-treatment) describes clusters of usually 3 to 5 bites in a zigzag and says bites usually heal within a week or two.
Bed bugs are not known to spread diseases to people, the CDC says; the trouble is itching, lost sleep, infection from scratching and, rarely, allergic reactions.

Difficult breathing, an irregular or forceful heartbeat, a swollen tongue, blisters (especially large ones), fever or feeling very sick after bites need immediate medical care, [the AAD](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/a-z/bed-bugs-symptoms) says.
To confirm bed bugs, look for dark spots, rusty stains, tiny eggs and pale shed skins along mattress seams and in bed frame cracks, as the EPA describes.

facts.caption: From the CDC, EPA, American Academy of Dermatology, Mayo Clinic, Cleveland Clinic, the University of Kentucky and Texas A&M, each linked on this page. Each clue is a lead, not proof.

body.text: What do bed bug bites look like?

Usually like itchy red welts or inflamed spots. [Mayo Clinic's bedbug page](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/bedbugs/symptoms-causes/syc-20370001) says bites are usually inflamed spots, often with a darker spot in the middle, itchy, arranged in a rough line or a cluster, and found on the face, neck, arms and hands. The [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/bed-bugs/about/index.html) describes a slightly swollen, red area that may itch, similar to a mosquito or flea bite, with marks that may be random or in a straight line.

body.alt: Magnified side view of a reddish-brown, oval, flat bed bug standing on pale human skin with fine hairs, its antennae and legs visible
body.caption: The biter: a common bed bug (Cimex lectularius) on human skin, magnified, in a CDC photograph; it is not shown feeding.
body.credit: CDC/ Donated by the World Health Organization, Geneva, Switzerland. (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: The [American Academy of Dermatology](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/a-z/bed-bugs-symptoms) says most people do not know they were bitten until the next day, when they notice several welts, often in a line that zigzags, welts that itch intensely, or specks of blood on the bedding. Its [diagnosis page](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/a-z/bed-bugs-treatment) adds that each cluster usually holds 3 to 5 bites in a zigzag. [Cleveland Clinic](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/17847-bedbugs) lists other looks: a pimple-like bump with a dark red center, a round blister of clear fluid, or hives, in a line, a zigzag or no pattern at all.

body.alt: A person's bare upper back and shoulders with about a dozen raised red welts scattered across the skin, some in small groups
body.caption: Bed bug bites as labeled by the emergency physician who photographed them, James Heilman, MD: red, raised welts scattered over a person's upper back and shoulders, some in small groups.
body.credit: James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: Not everyone gets marks. The CDC lists no physical signs at all among the possible signs of a bite, and the [University of Kentucky's bed bug fact sheet](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef636) says studies suggest about 30 percent of people do not react even when bitten repeatedly, with even less reaction among the elderly. So two people can share an infested bed and only one of them show bites.

body.alt: A forearm and wrist with dozens of small red bumps running in a long, branching row toward the hand
body.caption: A row of small red bumps along the outside of a left wrist and forearm, about four days old, that the photographer attributes to bed bugs; this is his own account, not a medical diagnosis.
body.credit: Oliver Arend, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

body.needed: Bed bug bites in a zigzag line or cluster on darker skin, from a medical or public-health source that confirmed bed bugs, beside a ruler marked in inches; public domain or CC0

body.text: Where on the body do bed bugs bite?

On whatever skin is uncovered while you sleep. Kentucky's fact sheet says bed bugs usually bite people at night while they sleep and feed on any skin exposed while sleeping, such as the face, neck, shoulders, back, arms and legs; the CDC adds the hands. Hungry bed bugs may also feed during the day, Kentucky says, especially if that is when the person normally sleeps.

The bugs do not stay on you. The AAD says bed bugs do not live on people: they come out of hiding to feed, which takes about 4 to 12 minutes, and then go back. The CDC says they inject an anesthetic and an anticoagulant that keep you from feeling the bite, and Mayo Clinic notes that bed bugs don't tend to burrow under clothing, so pajamas that cover as much skin as possible may help you avoid bites.
How soon do bed bug bites show up?

Usually within a few days, but sometimes not for two weeks. The CDC says most people do not notice marks until one to several days after the bite, and that marks may take as long as 14 days to develop in some people. Kentucky says many people get an itchy red welt within a day or so, while in others the reaction is delayed days or even weeks.

Reactions also change over time. The AAD says first bites may not itch right away because the body needs time to develop a reaction, that people tend to become more sensitive with repeated bites, and that someone bitten again and again during an infestation may get itchy welts within seconds.
What else looks like bed bug bites?

Plenty, which is why bites are a poor clue on their own. The [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/how-find-bed-bugs) says bed bug bites can look like bites from mosquitoes or chiggers, rashes such as eczema or fungal infections, or even hives, and that some people do not react at all. The AAD says people often blame mosquitoes, fleas or spiders, or mistake bites for an itchy rash, hives or chickenpox, and Mayo Clinic says bed bug bites can be hard to tell from other insect bites. These are the usual suspects, compared in the quick-ID table above.
Flea bites

Flea bites sit low. [Cleveland Clinic's flea bite page](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/21718-flea-bites) says they most often appear on the legs, especially the feet, calves and ankles, and rarely above the knee unless you spend a lot of time sitting or lying down; they are small bumps, sometimes with a ring around them, in a line or cluster, and they last only a few days. The [University of Kentucky's mystery bites guide](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef649) says fleas usually come with pets, but mice, rats, squirrels, skunks, opossums or raccoons can also bring them. [Flea bites](/blog/flea-bites) has photos.
Mosquito bites

A mosquito bite shows up fast. The [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/mosquitoes/about/about-mosquito-bites.html) says it can raise a puffy, reddish bump a few minutes after the bite, then a hard, itchy, reddish-brown bump or several bumps about a day later; some bites form small blisters or dark spots that look like bruises. Mosquitoes bite day and night, the [CDC's prevention page](https://www.cdc.gov/mosquitoes/prevention/index.html) says, and it advises screens on windows and doors with any holes repaired. [Bed bug bites vs mosquito bites](/blog/bed-bug-bites-vs-mosquito-bites) compares the two in detail.
Chigger bites

Chigger bites follow your clothes. [Cleveland Clinic's chigger page](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/23267-chigger-bites) describes a speckled line of red spots or pimples where clothing fits tightly, especially at waistbands, bra lines and sock lines or where skin folds, itching most in the first 24 to 48 hours and fading after about two weeks. Kentucky says chiggers live in tall weeds and dense vegetation, and that people may not connect the itch with being outdoors the day before. See [chigger bites](/blog/chigger-bites).
Scabies

Scabies is a rash caused by mites that live on people, as the AAD notes, not bites from a bug in the bed. The [CDC's scabies page](https://www.cdc.gov/scabies/signs-symptoms/index.html) lists intense itching, especially at night, and a pimple-like rash, often between the fingers and in the skin folds of the wrist, elbow, knee or armpit; after a first infestation, symptoms can take up to three to six weeks to appear. If you suspect scabies, the CDC says to contact your healthcare provider. See [scabies vs bed bugs](/blog/scabies-vs-bed-bugs).
Carpet beetle larvae and spiders

Neither is a likely bed biter. Carpet beetles do not bite, says [Texas A&M AgriLife's guide to mysterious bug bites](https://citybugs.tamu.edu/factsheets/biting-stinging/others/ent-3006-2/), but the hairs on their larvae irritate some people, and bite-like bumps can form where skin presses against a larva ([carpet beetle rash](/blog/carpet-beetle-rash)). Spider bites are rare, Texas A&M says, so they can be ruled out when someone has many bites, and Kentucky says that without the spider caught in the act, even a physician's diagnosis is little more than a guess ([what spider bites look like](/blog/what-does-a-spider-bite-look-like)).

If you keep getting bites but can find no bugs, [bites but no bed bugs](/blog/bed-bug-bites-but-no-bed-bugs) works through the other night biters, the [bug bite photo chart](/learn/bug-bites) sets the common bites side by side, and the [bug bite identifier](/tools/bug-bite-identifier) asks six questions about your bites.

body.text: How do you confirm the bites are from bed bugs?

Find the bugs or their signs; the bites cannot do it. The EPA calls bites on the skin a poor indicator of an infestation, and Kentucky's fact sheet says confirmation requires finding the bugs and/or their signs, which often takes a professional. The AAD says most people see only the signs, not the bugs. Mayo Clinic suggests inspecting at night, when bed bugs are active, and the CDC says they tend to live within 8 feet of where people sleep.

body.title: What confirms bed bugs
items: **Dark spots** about the size of a printed bullet point, which are bed bug excrement and may bleed into fabric like a marker, the EPA says.
**Rusty or reddish stains** on sheets or mattresses from crushed bed bugs (EPA); Mayo Clinic calls them small smears of blood.
**Eggs and eggshells**, white, oval and about 1/25 inch (1 mm) long, in cracks and crevices (EPA, AAD).
**Pale yellow shed skins**, left behind as young bed bugs molt five times on the way to adulthood (Mayo Clinic, EPA).
**Live bed bugs**: reddish-brown, flat and wingless, about 1/25 to 1/4 inch (1 to 7 mm) long; adults are about the size of an apple seed (CDC, Mayo Clinic).
**A sweet, musty odor** in a heavy infestation, though not everyone notices it, the AAD says; Kentucky says not to rely on smell.

body.alt: Close-up of a bed seam where dark mesh fabric meets brown upholstery, lined with reddish-brown bed bugs of several sizes and many tiny white eggs
body.caption: Bed bugs of several sizes and their white eggs along a seam of a bed, as the photographer described them: where an inspection starts.
body.credit: Charlysays, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

body.alt: Edge of a wooden bed-frame slat speckled with black ink-like spots, densest along the joint where two pieces of wood meet
body.caption: Bed bug fecal spots: black stains on a wooden bed frame near where bed bugs hid, photographed and described by the New York State IPM Program at Cornell University.
body.credit: NY State IPM Program at Cornell University, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

body.caption: The cast skin (molt) of a bed bug nymph on white fabric: hollow and split, with the empty leg casings still attached.
body.credit: (c) William Stephens, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: Look along the piping, seams and tags of the mattress and box spring and in cracks in the bed frame and headboard, the EPA says; a crack that will hold a credit card can hide a bed bug. Kentucky's fact sheet describes interceptors, small plastic dishes set under bed and furniture legs that wandering bed bugs fall into, and says a trap under each bed leg also forms a barrier that can help reduce bites. [Signs of bed bugs](/blog/signs-of-bed-bugs-checklist), [bed bug poop](/blog/bed-bug-poop), [where bed bugs hide](/blog/where-do-bed-bugs-hide) and [what bed bugs look like](/blog/what-do-bed-bugs-look-like) go further, and a [companion guide to bed bug bites](/blog/bed-bug-bites) covers whether a single bite means an infestation.
How long do bed bug bites last?

Usually a week or two. The AAD and Mayo Clinic both say bed bug bites usually heal and go away within a week or two, and Mayo Clinic says that happens without treatment; Cleveland Clinic says they usually heal within a week but can last longer, depending on how your body reacts. Bites keep coming while the bugs remain: the AAD says getting rid of the bed bugs is the only way to stop the bites.

body.needed: Bed bug bites on the face or neck a few days old, photographed for a medical or public-health source that confirmed bed bugs, with the date and a ruler marked in inches; public domain or CC0

body.text: Do bed bugs spread disease?

They are not known to. The CDC says bed bugs are not known to spread diseases to people, and Kentucky says that although they can harbor various pathogens, transmission to humans has not been proven and is considered unlikely. The harm is real but different: the CDC lists itching, lost sleep, insomnia and anxiety, and says intense itching can lead to excessive scratching and possibly a secondary skin infection.

Allergic reactions are possible, the CDC adds, with enlarged bite marks, painful swelling at the bite and, on rare occasions, anaphylaxis. The AAD says anemia can rarely develop in someone who gets numerous bites.
How do you treat bed bug bites?

Most bites need only simple care at home. The AAD's treatment page says that if there are no signs of an infection or a serious reaction, you can often treat the bites at home: wash them with soap and water, which helps prevent a skin infection and reduces itchiness, and apply a corticosteroid cream if they itch. A weak form is sold without a prescription; stronger ones need one.

The CDC recommends antiseptic creams or lotions for the itch and not scratching, to prevent a secondary infection, and says an antihistamine may help people with itchy inflammatory reactions. Mayo Clinic's [diagnosis and treatment page](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/bedbugs/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20370005) says bites usually need no treatment and lists a hydrocortisone skin cream or an oral antihistamine to ease symptoms.
When should you see a doctor for bed bug bites?

See a doctor for many bites, blisters, signs of infection or an allergic reaction. The AAD advises seeing a dermatologist if you have many bites, blisters, a skin infection (bites that feel tender or ooze discharge such as pus) or an allergic skin reaction (red, swollen skin or hives). The CDC says to speak with your healthcare provider if you think you are having an allergic reaction, Mayo Clinic says the same for allergic or severe skin reactions, and Cleveland Clinic adds severe itching that keeps you from going about your day.

body.title: Get medical care right away
body.text: The American Academy of Dermatology lists these as serious reactions to bed bug bites that require immediate medical care: difficult breathing, an irregular or forceful heartbeat, a swollen tongue, blisters (especially large ones), fever, feeling very sick, infection from scratching, and anemia, which is rare but can develop with numerous bites.
What should you do if it is bed bugs?

Treat the bed bugs, not just the bites. The AAD says that if you find signs of bed bugs, call a pest-control company or your property manager, and that you should not use bug spray or a fogger, which have little effect on bed bugs. The CDC also points people to a professional pest control company experienced with bed bugs. [The bed bug elimination plan](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-bed-bugs) and [the complete guide to bed bugs](/learn/bed-bugs) cover the steps, and [bed bugs in hotels](/blog/bed-bugs-in-hotels) covers checking a room when you travel, since the CDC says people who travel frequently face a higher risk.

body.title: Keep the evidence
body.text: Photograph the bites beside a ruler marked in inches, with the date, and seal any bug you catch in a small jar. Your county Cooperative Extension office can help identify the bug, and your healthcare provider can look at the bite photos.

faqs.question: Do bed bug bites always come in threes?
faqs.answer: No. The American Academy of Dermatology says bed bug bites often appear in clusters of usually 3 to 5 bites in a zigzag pattern, but the CDC says the marks may also be random or appear in a straight line, and Mayo Clinic describes a rough line or a cluster. No pattern proves bed bugs: the EPA calls bites a poor indicator of an infestation, so look for the bugs, their dark spots, eggs and shed skins before you decide.

faqs.question: What do bed bug bites look like when they first appear?
faqs.answer: Often like nothing at first. The CDC says the bite itself is not felt because bed bugs inject an anesthetic, and that most people do not notice marks until one to several days later, though they can take as long as 14 days. The American Academy of Dermatology says first-time bites may not itch right away, and that when welts do appear they itch intensely and often run in a zigzag line. Some people never show marks at all.

faqs.question: Why do I have bites but my partner doesn't?
faqs.answer: Often because people react differently. The University of Kentucky says studies suggest about 30 percent of people do not react even when bitten repeatedly, and that the share is even higher among the elderly, while the CDC says bed bug bites affect each person differently and can leave no physical signs. The American Academy of Dermatology adds that people tend to become more sensitive to bites the more often they are bitten.

faqs.question: Can you feel a bed bug bite?
faqs.answer: Usually not. The CDC says bed bugs inject fluids, an anesthetic and an anticoagulant, that keep you from feeling the bite when it happens, and the University of Kentucky says the bite is painless, so people seldom realize they are being bitten. The American Academy of Dermatology says a bed bug feeds for about 4 to 12 minutes and then goes back into hiding; it does not live on your body.

faqs.question: Can you get bed bug bites during the day?
faqs.answer: Yes, though night is typical. The University of Kentucky says bed bugs usually bite people at night while they are sleeping, but that hungry bed bugs may also feed during the day, especially if that is when the person normally sleeps. The CDC says they hide during the day in mattress seams, box springs, bed frames, headboards and cracks near the bed, and tend to stay within 8 feet of where people sleep.

faqs.question: Does one bed bug bite mean you have an infestation?
faqs.answer: Not on its own. The EPA says bites on the skin are a poor indicator of a bed bug infestation because they can look like mosquito or chigger bites, rashes or hives, and the University of Kentucky says confirmation requires finding the bugs or their signs. If you wake with bites, check the mattress seams, box spring and bed frame for dark spots, rusty stains, tiny white eggs, pale shed skins or live bugs before you treat for bed bugs.

faqs.question: Can bed bug bites turn into blisters?
faqs.answer: Yes, in some people. Cleveland Clinic lists a round bump filled with clear fluid among the common looks of a bed bug bite, and Mayo Clinic says an allergic reaction can include severe itching, blisters or hives. The American Academy of Dermatology advises seeing a dermatologist for blisters and lists blisters, especially large blisters, among the serious reactions that require immediate medical care, along with difficult breathing, a swollen tongue and fever.

faqs.question: How do I know if it's bed bugs or fleas?
faqs.answer: Look at where the bites are and what else is around. Cleveland Clinic says flea bites most often appear on the feet, calves and ankles and rarely above the knee, while the CDC says bed bug bites show up on the face, neck, arms, hands or other body parts after sleeping. Fleas usually come with a pet or with wildlife such as mice, squirrels or raccoons, the University of Kentucky says, while bed bugs leave dark spots, eggs and shed skins in the bed, as the EPA describes.

faqs.question: Will bug spray stop bed bug bites?
faqs.answer: No. The American Academy of Dermatology says you should not use bug spray or a fogger against bed bugs because these products have little effect on them, and that getting rid of the bed bugs is the only way to stop the bites. If you find signs of bed bugs, the AAD says to call a pest-control company or your property manager, and the CDC points to a professional pest control company experienced in treating bed bugs.

faqs.question: Do bed bugs bite pets?
faqs.answer: They can. The CDC says bed bugs bite people and animals at night while they sleep, feeding on their blood, though Mayo Clinic says humans are their preferred host and that they hide in the cracks and crevices around beds. Whoever is bitten, the University of Kentucky says confirmation requires finding the bugs or their signs, such as the dark spots, eggs and shed skins the EPA describes. Ask a veterinarian about any rash on a pet.
